common_name: Blushing Bride Hydrangea (Endless Summer Collection White-to-Pink Reblooming Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Blushing Bride flowers on both old and new wood, so late-season pruning or a hard freeze that kills old buds still leaves a fall rebloom on new growth.

directions: Blushing Bride is a member of the Endless Summer Collection bred by Bailey Nurseries, selected as a white-flowered companion to the original Endless Summer. Large mophead blooms open nearly pure white and slowly blush soft pink at the petal edges as they age, staying a clean white in more neutral-to-alkaline soil and developing stronger pink tones with garden lime; unlike most macrophylla cultivars its white base color does not shift blue in acidic soil. Because it reblooms on new wood as well as old, it tolerates late-winter cold damage or renewal pruning far better than antique mopheads, though for the fullest first flush prune only lightly right after the initial bloom to preserve old-wood buds. Give it partial shade and consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since the large leaves wilt quickly in Gulf Coast afternoon sun and summer heat.

common_name: Summer Crush Hydrangea (Compact Endless Summer Collection Raspberry-Red to Purple Reblooming Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Summer Crush is compact enough for containers and small borders and reblooms on new wood, so light shaping does not sacrifice the whole season's flowers.

directions: Summer Crush is a dwarf addition to the Endless Summer Collection from Bailey Nurseries, bred for a tight 1.5 to 2.5 foot mounded habit that suits containers, small-space gardens, and mass plantings where full-size mopheads are too large. Its dense mophead blooms open a vivid raspberry-red in neutral-to-alkaline soil and shift toward magenta-purple with added soil acidity, giving noticeably more saturated color than older reblooming cultivars. Because it flowers on both old and new wood, plants damaged by a late freeze or pruned hard in spring still produce a strong late-summer flush. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich, and provide afternoon shade in the Gulf Coast heat, since the compact form has a smaller root system and dries out faster than larger cultivars.

common_name: Let's Dance Diva Hydrangea (Large-Flowered Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Let's Dance Diva is a Proven Winners reblooming bigleaf hydrangea bred for exceptionally large flower heads on a compact plant that flowers on both old and new wood.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in the Gulf South. Let's Dance Diva is part of the Proven Winners Let's Dance series and stands out among its series relatives for unusually large, dense mophead flower clusters on a plant that otherwise keeps the same compact, rounded habit under 3 feet tall. Like Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue, it flowers reliably on new growth as well as on old wood, so a late freeze that damages the previous year's stems does not eliminate the season's bloom the way it can on older mophead cultivars. Flower color shifts from blue in acidic soil to pink to purple-red in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments, particularly aluminum sulfate to hold a truer blue. Deadhead spent blooms and prune only lightly to shape in late winter, avoiding heavy cuts that would remove the current season's developing flower buds.

common_name: Peachy Knock Out Rose (Landscape Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0-6.5), fertile soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours direct sun); like other Knock Out roses, Peachy Knock Out needs full sun for reliable, continuous bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun. Peachy Knock Out is one of the newer additions to the Knock Out rose family, distinguished by warm peachy-apricot single blooms that fade toward a softer cream at the petal edges as each flower ages, a color unlike the reds, pinks, and yellows of the earlier Knock Out releases. It shares the same essentially disease-immune performance against black spot and powdery mildew, self-cleaning habit that drops spent flowers without deadheading, and continuous bloom from spring until hard frost that made the original Knock Out the best-selling landscape rose in America. Its compact, rounded habit fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and mass plantings where a smaller-scale Knock Out is wanted. Prune in late winter by cutting the entire plant back by about a third to a half to stimulate vigorous new growth and maximum bloom; no deadheading or fungicide spraying is required for a healthy plant.

common_name: You and Me Together Hydrangea (Reblooming Pink-to-Blue Mophead Bred by Michael Dirr)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Together blooms on old and new wood, so it recovers a rebloom flush even after a hard late-winter pruning or cold snap.

directions: Together is the lead introduction in the You and Me series, a group of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas bred by noted horticulturist Michael Dirr and marketed by Bailey Nurseries alongside siblings such as Romance, Forever, and Expression. It produces large, tightly domed mophead flowers in soft pink on alkaline soil and clear blue on acidic soil, with sturdy stems bred to hold the heavy flower heads upright without flopping. Because it sets buds on both old and new wood, gardeners north of its old-wood-hardy range still get a reliable late-summer bloom even after winter dieback. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich in partial shade, and mulch to buffer root-zone temperature swings, since large-leaved reblooming mopheads wilt quickly in dry heat.

common_name: Miss Saori Hydrangea (RHS Chelsea Plant of the Century, Pink-Edged Double White Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Miss Saori blooms primarily on old wood, so prune only right after flowering and protect stems from hard late-winter freezes to keep the flower buds intact.

directions: Miss Saori was bred by Japanese hydrangea specialist Ryoji Irie and became the first hydrangea named RHS Chelsea Flower Show Plant of the Century in 2013. Its double, star-shaped florets open white with a distinct rose-pink picotee edge that deepens as the mophead blooms age, a bicolor pattern that holds regardless of soil pH since it comes from petal pigmentation rather than aluminum uptake. Flowers form mainly on the previous season's wood, so limit pruning to shaping cuts made immediately after bloom and avoid removing old stems in fall or winter. Give it partial shade and evenly moist, humus-rich soil, since both the large leaves and the long-lasting double flowers are prone to wilting in dry heat or strong afternoon sun.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Zebra blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering and site it where the near-black stems are visible against a light-colored wall or fence in winter.

directions: Zebra is grown as much for its striking near-black, purple-toned stems banded with green as for its blooms, which are flat lacecap heads of tiny fertile blue-to-purple florets ringed by larger white-to-pale-pink sterile florets. The strong stem contrast is most dramatic on leafless winter wood, making it a good choice sited where bare stems catch winter light. Flowers form on old wood, so prune only to remove dead or damaged stems right after the summer bloom, never in fall or winter, or the following year's flower buds are lost. Give it partial shade and consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since both stem color and lacecap bloom quality fade in hot, dry, full-sun conditions typical of the Gulf Coast summer.

common_name: Fuji Waterfall Hydrangea (Fuji no Taki, Cascading Double-Row White Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Fuji Waterfall blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering, and its cascading habit shows best planted where the flower heads can spill over a wall, slope, or container edge.

directions: Fuji Waterfall, known in Japan as Fuji no Taki, is a mountain hydrangea prized for double and triple rows of frilled, lacy white sterile florets that ring each flat flower head and cascade downward under their own weight, giving the plant its waterfall name. Unlike single-row lacecaps, the extra rows of sterile florets stay showy for weeks and age to soft pink or blue depending on soil pH. As a serrata, it is more sun- and cold-tolerant than most macrophylla lacecaps and blooms on old wood, so limit pruning to shaping cuts made immediately after flowering. Partial shade and moderate, evenly moist soil keep the airy flower heads from scorching, and a lightly sheltered spot protects the pendant blooms from wind damage.

common_name: Blaumeise Hydrangea (Blue Tit, Teller Series Blue-to-Rose Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Blaumeise blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to protect the following year's buds.

directions: Blaumeise, sold in English-speaking markets as Blue Tit, is a member of the Swiss-bred Teller series of lacecap hydrangeas selected for exceptionally strong, saturated flower color. Flat lacecap heads carry tiny fertile florets surrounded by larger sterile florets that turn a deep true blue in acidic soil and shift to rich rose-pink in neutral-to-alkaline soil, with color intensity that stays stronger through the season than many older lacecap cultivars. Like most macrophylla, it flowers primarily on old wood, so prune only lightly right after bloom and avoid cutting back stems in fall or winter. Give it partial shade and consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since large leaves and lacecap flowers wilt quickly in Gulf Coast afternoon heat.

common_name: Editor Blumhardt Hydrangea (New Zealand Deep Blue-to-Pink Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Editor Blumhardt blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to protect the following year's buds.

directions: Editor Blumhardt is a lacecap bigleaf hydrangea raised in New Zealand and named for a longtime editor of the New Zealand Gardener magazine, and it remains a mainstay of Australasian hydrangea collections. Its flat flower heads carry a dense center of small fertile florets ringed by larger sterile florets that turn deep violet-blue in acidic soil and rich pink-red in neutral-to-alkaline soil, with unusually vivid saturation for a lacecap. It blooms on old wood, so limit pruning to shaping cuts made right after flowering rather than in fall or winter. Give it partial shade and consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since the large leaves and open lacecap flowers wilt quickly in hot, dry conditions typical of the Gulf Coast summer.
